title: Legal Aid of North Carolina (Gilchrist, Campbell, Wisner) with LawDroid — LIA, tiered access, and the modernised-intake model at LSC ITC 2025
pub: LSC Innovations in Technology Conference 2025 (Phoenix), streamed session, LSC YouTube channel
author: Scheree Gilchrist · Andre Campbell · Jacob Wisner · Tom Martin

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s implementation-focused proposition and extends it with a concrete legal-aid delivery model: automate suitable intake and referral work while preserving human support, using multidisciplinary partnerships and designing solutions for replication. It describes programme goals and organisation, however, rather than demonstrating improved access, quality or efficiency.
qs: All of this is being done to ensure that the clients that need the human support can still get the support they need, but that some of the work that humans don't need to do gets done in a very efficient way.

One of the things that we were very mindful of when we were creating the innovation lab is that we're creating solutions that are scalable and that can be easily replicated by any program provider across the country.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts selective, human-led deployment and materially extends the cluster with a concrete legal-aid operating model: routine intake is assigned to technology, complex needs escalate to staff, and value depends on redesigned roles, referral governance, system integration and maintained human channels. It also appropriately limits its claims because implementation is incomplete and outcome effects have not yet been evaluated.
qs: The idea is to allow the tech to do the things that tech do best.
So that is all part of the model and the process change that will happen beyond the tech integrations that are happening.

kp.k: Tiered access reserves human expertise for higher-skill work
kp.d: Gilchrist presents a human-centered access model combining AI, self-help, automation and referrals at the entry level, with paralegal and attorney intervention as clients progress. Its pyramid describes service-access tiers, not firm staffing leverage. The integrated model is a preview rather than a fully implemented system, and its intended benefit is more effective use of scarce human capacity.
qs: Our conversation today will focus on previewing, and I emphasize that word, we're previewing a tiered access system that integrates AI, self-help resources, automated tools, and coordinated referrals.
And the human interventions are designed to allow our staff or paralegals and our attorneys to work at the top end of their skillset.
It's not fully developed yet, it's not fully implemented yet.

kp.k: Demand motivates redesign, but call counts conflict
kp.d: Gilchrist reports about 450 staff and '200 and odd attorneys' yet substantial access pressures, initially citing 400,000 helpline calls and 12,000 applications. Martin also uses 400,000 calls, whereas Jacob later cites 800,000 calls and 12,000 online intakes. No period or reconciliation is supplied. Campbell describes callers waiting 25–30 minutes and then spending 15 minutes in conversation before learning they are ineligible.
qs: We have about 450 staff.
And we have about 200 and odd attorneys.
The number of calls that are coming in to our helpline, 400,000, 12,000 applications, clients demanding quick and easy access to our services.
We're attempting to help alleviate the 800,000 calls, 12,000 online intakes, but also there's a coverage and an access issue we can try to solve with some of the same technologies.

kp.k: Client portal combines screening, resources and progress tracking
kp.d: Campbell describes a developing portal that explains service scope and eligibility, provides resources and chatbot access, and tracks requests through conflict checks, financial checks and approval rather than merely requesting a callback. He reports reducing application and demographic entry to about two and a half minutes, with further client testing planned; no sample size or testing method is given. API integration is intended to prevent duplicate entry into the case management system.
qs: It is not just somewhere you go to sign up to have someone call you back.
I've created my request, I'm past conflict check, my financial information has been checked, and now I have been approved.
We have gotten this down to about two and a half minutes from the time you click to come on our website to actually fill out your application and your demographics about who you are, et cetera.
So if it's already in the portal, it can be ported to the case management system so it's there and they don't have to retype it.

kp.k: LIA delivers source-grounded legal information around the clock
kp.d: LawDroid founder Tom Martin describes the existing assistant, called Leah in the transcript, as using legal-domain experts' materials with a configured retrieval pipeline and Claude Sonnet 3.5. He reports 16,000 conversations, including eviction and domestic violence inquiries, and continuous availability. Reduced pressure on staff is presented as a possible benefit, not a measured result; model selection is framed as use-case dependent rather than a pursuit of the newest model.
qs: In this case, the model that we're using is Claude Sonnet 3.5 but I would also point out that you don't necessarily wanna use the latest, greatest model.
It's really about the model that fits your use case.
16,000 conversations have taken place with Leah.
And so in that way, she's available 24/7/365.
they can reach out and get that information preliminarily from Leah, which could also help to lessen the burden on the staff of those 400,000 calls.

kp.k: Concierge expansion targets preliminary eligibility and accessible interaction
kp.d: Martin describes a planned extension from answering questions to preliminary eligibility screening, including explanations of the screening process itself. He states that the assistant responds automatically in English or Spanish. Gilchrist clarifies that the current website interaction requires typing and that spoken interaction is an intended accessibility expansion, prompted by feedback about typing difficulties and intimidation.
qs: So the concierge is an extension of Leah acting as a knowledge assistant to go beyond just answering questions to determining preliminary eligibility.
it could help to answer the questions about the very process they're going through.
She can interact in English and Spanish.
Right now you have to type your question in when you're interacting with Leah on our website.
So one of the expansions is to have Leah speak and communicate with people.

kp.k: Attorney review and feedback drive iterative AI improvement
kp.d: Martin reports attorneys reviewing answers and supplying specific feedback, followed by prompt engineering and retrieval-pipeline adjustments. Questions also exposed gaps in existing legal materials, prompting source expansion. The system collects response ratings, overall experience ratings and unanswered questions. These are described as quality-control practices, not quantified accuracy findings or a statement that every client-facing answer receives advance human verification.
qs: We had attorneys within Lance that were reviewing the answers and giving very specific feedback about how to adjust the answers.
And on our side, we adjusted the model with prompt engineering and also modifying part of the pipeline to make it answer more appropriately.
And then the source material was expanded upon to answer those questions that weren't yet answered.
We also have a little thumbs up or thumbs down on each response where we can gather a sentiment of was this a good answer or was it not a good answer?
And we also log whenever the bot says I don't know and it does sometimes say I don't know because the information is not in the source material yet.

kp.k: Knowledge maintenance uses existing subject-matter review processes
kp.d: Gilchrist explains that annual review of resource materials predates the AI assistant. A former management attorney coordinates updates and assigns supervisors to check legal changes. Martin says the platform allows organizational staff to update material directly without going through LawDroid, and reports that staff uploaded Hurricane Helene information within about 24 hours, enabling the assistant to answer related questions.
qs: At the end of each year, we do a review through our centralized intake unit.
She'll make assignments to supervisors to just check off on has there been any updates in the law that she might not be aware of.
This is one where there's actually a platform that you have an account for, you access, and you can update it.

within about 24 hours of Hurricane Helene, one of the staff members was able to upload on their own, not going through us, but new information that would answer questions about how to deal with the after effects of Hurricane Helene.

kp.d: Gilchrist announces a Duke Center on Law and Technology case study to evaluate the assistant and AI integrations, track data and develop benchmarks; no results are presented. Asked whether AI information provision reduced advice cases, she explicitly says case-number impacts have not yet been examined. She dates implementation to June or July of the previous year and proposes comparing July–December 2023 with July–December 2024. Intake reporting and geographic mapping are also still being developed.
qs: We are doing a case study with the Duke Center on Law and Technology.
They're gonna be tracking the data. They're gonna be identifying trends and stories as well as coming up with some benchmarks for us as legal services providers to use.
Leah was implemented June, July of last year and so we've not looked at the impact on case numbers yet.
We'll do a year-over-year analysis from 2023 July to December and what July to December 2024 did and then we'll be able to actively answer that question.

kp.k: Trusted referrals broaden access beyond one provider's services
kp.d: Gilchrist frames the developing trusted partner network as a way to address legal, social and human needs through vetted bidirectional referrals rather than expecting one legal aid organization to meet every need. Jacob describes 'no wrong door' access through familiar local organizations. The legal network starts with Legal Aid of North Carolina and six partners, reportedly covering around four million total clients across five case management systems; a separate community partnership pilot concerns expunctions and workforce development.
qs: Where they can make referrals to us, we can make referrals to them.
And there's no wrong door, even if that's not the point they're going to receive assistance from.

Starting including us and six other partners, Pisgah Legal Services, Charlotte Center for Legal Advocacy, Land Loss Prevention Project, Financial Protection Law Center, North Carolina Justice Center, and Disability Rights NC.
And combined, we cover around four million total clients across North Carolina and work in five different case management systems.
we have identified a community partner using expunctions as our pilot model and we're working with workforce development in our state to launch that.

kp.k: Referral success depends on governance and local trust
kp.d: Jacob emphasizes that technical connections alone are insufficient: partners must agree on case scope, capacity, response expectations, notifications and information exchange. Where direct case management integration is unavailable, partner portals are planned for making and tracking referrals. During disaster response, electronic referrals reportedly supplied around 5% of current caseload, and most listed technical changes were completed within the first week. He nevertheless stresses that residents' trust in local organizations remains essential.
qs: Do they have two days, do they have three days? Will they get a notification if they've sent something that we have or haven't accepted it? What information will we be sending to each other?
each partner's capacities and scopes must be understood, clearly communicated, and respected.
where that's not an option, the partner has to be able to get into their own portal.
Direct electronic referrals from sister organizations, which had been disused, went online quickly and we've received around 5% of our current caseload through that system
And most of these things were done within the first week after the disaster.
And so this taught us how essential and helpful it is to have local partners, partners across the state.

kp.k: Staff augmentation and phone access remain explicit commitments
kp.d: The panel states that intake staff have not been displaced and that phone service will remain for clients unable or unwilling to use digital alternatives. Gilchrist describes possible repurposing of intake specialists as case managers with broader client-support and coordination duties beyond data entry, escalating matters requiring legal intervention to attorneys. Paralegals retain a human checking role, including difficult conflict checks.
qs: we are gonna still allow the phone service to be there for those clients who cannot, will not, and should not be using something else.
we have not displaced them.
the idea is not to use AI or any of the tech solutions that you're seeing to replace staff.
So beyond just what the intake person does which is data entry, allow the case manager to be sort of a goal between the attorney and the applicant or the paralegal and the applicant.
And they will do some of the things that the machine can't do, like conflict check-in, which can be hard and difficult

kp.k: Digital access can overwhelm downstream processing capacity
kp.d: Jacob cautions that online intake scales only if demand is understood and managed. He reports that the organization's first online intake iteration had to be shut down after receiving more applications in one week than staff could process in a month. The example qualifies expectations that easier entry alone resolves access constraints; the partner network likewise requires explicit agreement about what each participant can accept.
qs: If you can figure out and manage your demand, online portals and online intakes can scale, but you won't always get it right.
I know we had to shut down our online intake, the first ever iteration of it, the first time we put it on, just 'cause we received in a week more applications than we could process in a month.
determining the capacities, scopes and what people can accept is part of the process.

kp.k: Implementation requires dedicated management, phased funding and experimentation
kp.d: Campbell recommends dedicated project management, feasibility assessment and consultation across clients, lawyers, paralegals, intake staff and leadership rather than designing around one group's preferences. Martin recommends starting with narrow, repetitive information needs and expanding iteratively. Gilchrist describes a three-year grant-funded process: initial portal and partner-network work, followed by phone-system changes and consideration of a mobile app and walk-in processes. The team intends solutions to be replicable by other legal service providers, but does not present evidence of replication outcomes.
qs: It should not be a part-time event that somebody takes up within the environment
Find a way to communicate with the clients, with the lawyers, the paralegals, the intake, the CEO, the CIO, the chief tech.
you don't have to start with everything, you could start small.
It's a three year grant, so it will be developing and it's in phases.
So phase one is what you're seeing now, which is the online intake portal and the trusted partner network.
we're creating solutions that are scalable and that can be easily replicated by any program provider across the country.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Gilchrist presents AI-enabled tiered access as a way to automate routine work while reserving human support for tasks requiring professional skills, not as a staff-replacement programme.
pts.d: Scheree Gilchrist describes a proposed service-access pathway combining AI, self-help, automated tools and referrals. Attorneys and paralegals would enter as clients need higher-skilled assistance; paralegals would remain responsible for difficult tasks such as conflict checking. She explicitly rejects replacing staff, while proposing possible repurposing of intake specialists into case managers with broader client-support duties. The pyramid describes tiers of client access, not a law firm's staffing structure.

pts.k: Martin says LIA provides continuous preliminary legal information and could reduce pressure on the helpline.
pts.d: Tom Martin describes the existing assistant, called Leah or LEA in the transcript, as a conversational knowledge assistant drawing on legal-aid domain experts' materials rather than materials developed by LawDroid. It has handled questions about eviction, domestic violence and other issues. He claims round-the-clock access allows people to obtain preliminary information when calls cannot be answered promptly, but frames staff-burden reduction as a possibility rather than a measured outcome.

pts.k: Martin predicts an AI concierge will identify preliminary eligibility earlier and explain the intake process interactively.
pts.d: The proposed concierge extends LIA beyond answering substantive information questions to guiding applicants through eligibility questions and explaining those questions as they arise. Martin argues that this could avoid frustration from learning late in intake that the organisation cannot help. He describes preliminary screening, not final autonomous eligibility decisions or replacement of legal advice.

pts.k: Martin and Gilchrist identify multilingual interaction and planned voice access as ways to reduce accessibility barriers.
pts.d: Martin says LIA already responds in English and Spanish, automatically matching a user's language. Gilchrist distinguishes the current typed website interaction from a planned spoken interface, intended to help people who cannot comfortably type a question or find entering a legal question into a chatbot intimidating.

pts.k: Martin claims source-grounded AI can expose gaps in legal information and support rapid updates without vendor intervention.
pts.d: Martin reports that testing revealed questions absent from existing webpages, brochures and other source documents, prompting expansion of those materials. He describes this as a feedback loop improving both the knowledge base and the assistant. He also says the no-code platform lets legal-aid staff update content themselves, citing a Hurricane Helene information update within about 24 hours as an operational example.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists principally of implementation experience and usage counts; reduced workloads or changes in advice-case numbers had not yet been measured.
pts.d: Martin reports 16,000 conversations without specifying a measurement window or unique-user count. Speakers cite demand pressures of 400,000 helpline calls and 12,000 applications; Jacob later gives 800,000 calls and 12,000 online intakes, leaving the call-volume discrepancy unresolved. Campbell reports an approximately two-and-a-half-minute portal application process, but this concerns the broader portal rather than a demonstrated AI effect. Gilchrist explicitly says the impact on case numbers is not yet known. The session therefore supplies operational examples, not completed causal evidence of reduced demand or improved legal outcomes.

pts.k: Martin bases reliability claims on attorney review, constrained source retrieval and iterative feedback; Gilchrist announces future external evaluation.
pts.d: Martin describes attorneys reviewing answers and giving specific feedback, followed by prompt and retrieval-pipeline changes. User thumbs-up/down responses, overall ratings and logged 'I don't know' answers provide additional feedback. These are described as quality-control mechanisms, not published accuracy scores; the session does not establish that an attorney checks every live response before a user receives it. Gilchrist says a Duke Center on Law and Technology case study will evaluate LIA and the AI integrations and develop benchmarks, but presents no completed results.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The session distinguishes an operating knowledge assistant from a still-developing, three-year modernisation programme.
pts.d: At the 2025 conference, Gilchrist dates LIA's implementation to June or July of the preceding year, meaning 2024. The expanded concierge, voice interface and integrated access model are previews rather than fully implemented services. She describes a three-year grant with online intake and trusted partnerships in phase one, followed by phone-system changes and consideration of mobile and walk-in access. A July–December 2023 versus July–December 2024 comparison of case numbers is planned, not reported.

pts.k: The speakers condition successful adoption on suitable source materials, human oversight, project management, demand management and partner capacity.
pts.d: Martin says model choice must fit the use case—Claude Sonnet 3.5 in this implementation—and documents must be organised for retrieval. Gilchrist describes an existing annual resource-review process involving legal supervisors. Campbell stresses dedicated project management and consultation across clients and staff. Jacob warns that easier online access can overwhelm processing capacity, citing the shutdown of an earlier intake version. The referral component also depends on agreement about scope, capacity, information exchange and response obligations; its benefits should not be attributed to AI alone.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The intended beneficiaries are people seeking civil legal aid, including those needing self-help, referrals or non-digital access, and the staff supporting them.
pts.d: The model concerns access to justice for low-income individuals and families in North Carolina, not enterprise legal spending. Users could obtain information without applying for representation, learn about eligibility earlier, or reach other legal and community organisations. Campbell expects digital options to free phone capacity for people who cannot or should not use them, while retaining intake staff. Gilchrist proposes broader support roles for some staff and higher-skilled work for lawyers and paralegals. She also presents the tools as intended for replication by other legal-service programmes. LawDroid is the technology vendor; Legal Aid of North Carolina and referral partners deliver services.
